1:
The opening Hallelujah is disputed before the psalm begins. Charles Ellicott says the short doxology does not strictly form part of the psalm, since the alphabetical arrangement starts with the words that follow. John Gill gives the same argument and draws the opposite conclusion, that it is the title, expressive of the subject matter, and stands so in the versions — as it should, since the psalm is alphabetical and the first letter of the word is the fifth and not the first of the alphabet; he notes that one version omits it. Adam Clarke says the psalm has no title in the Hebrew unless this word be considered as such, and sets out the structure: the first eight verses have two members each and the last two three, making twenty-two hemistichs in all, one for each letter. But the received division into verses, he adds, is not proper, since Hebrew poetry requires that every hemistich stand by itself and carry a complete sense. Keil and Delitzsch place the psalm at the head of a trilogy and pair it with the next, which they call twin in form and in contents, both sententious, both alphabetical, both twenty-two lines of mostly three words each; and they remark drily of one critic who transposed verses and emended a word that in the warmth of his zeal he ran against the boundary-posts of the letters without observing them.

John Calvin supplies the liturgical setting: this psalm and those that follow it are supposed to have been sung by the Jews at the Passover, and the hymn in question is in all likelihood the one our Lord sang with his disciples after the Last Supper. He reports considerable discrepancy among the Jews about which psalms made up the greater collection, the various opinions extending or contracting its range widely, and calls those traditions uncertain and ill defined, having more respect to the sayings of the Rabbins than to the internal evidence of Scripture — which he then proposes to examine, beginning from the fact that nearly all the psalms in the range carry this same word. Augustine of Hippo hears the word as belonging to a season: the days have come for us to sing it, days which come only to pass away, and which typify the day that neither comes nor passes, when all the troubles of this life have been shut out.

On praising with the whole heart Adam Clarke insists on the adverb, that the heart must be employed without division or distraction, and distinguishes two settings named in the verse, the secret assembly, meaning private meetings for the communion of saints, and the general congregation; such private meetings, he says, have existed ever since God had a church on earth. Matthew Henry makes the same division and adds the principle, that what duty we call others to we must oblige ourselves to first. C.H. Spurgeon puts it as example rather than exhortation, that the best way to enforce an exhortation is to set one, though the example must be of the best kind or we lead others to do the work limping. On the works being sought out Adam Clarke takes the verb as investigated and carefully examined, by every genuine philosopher and lover of nature who traces the great First Cause through his works, and promises that such a man will be astonished at the perfections of the Creator. Charles Ellicott agrees that they are the object of meditation and enquiry, thinks the psalmist had historical proofs in view but allows the words a wide range, and finds the best illustration in Ruskin’s warnings to his own generation against insensibility to natural beauty. John Wesley compresses it to diligent meditation, and John Gill runs through the works to be meditated on, from creation and providence to the work of grace upon the heart.
4:
How the wonderful works are made to be remembered is answered four ways. Charles Ellicott gives the literal sense, that God has made a memorial for his wonderful works. John Gill lists the memorials: things in nature stand as they were from the beginning, the sun and stars keeping their course and the seasons their round; remarkable providences have been carefully recorded and handed to posterity; the deliverance out of Egypt was annually remembered in the passover, the feeding in the wilderness by a pot of manna preserved in the tabernacle, and redemption in the ordinance appointed for that purpose. Adam Clarke makes the works themselves the memorial: he who seeks them out will never forget them, since everything of God’s framing is done in such a way as to strike the imagination, interest the senses, and charm and edify the intellect. He adds that the psalmist may principally intend the deliverance from the Babylonish captivity, which the psalm is supposed to celebrate. John Wesley says the same shorter, that they are remembered by their own nature and by the lasting benefits flowing from them.

The word rendered meat divides the entry. Charles Ellicott notes that it often means prey, from its being torn as by a wild beast, but that it is used elsewhere in the plain sense of food, so there need be no allusion to the spoils of the Canaanite wars — though he grants that the next verse makes such an allusion exceedingly probable, and refers the reader to a dictionary article on the word. Adam Clarke keeps the prey and widens it: the word signifies what is taken in hunting, whether wild beasts, venison or fowl, and also spoil taken from enemies; he suggests the quails in the wilderness, and then applies it to the support given during the captivity, by which God proved himself mindful of his covenant and faithful to his promises. John Gill allows the spoil of the Egyptians or the manna, and then divides the meat into corporeal and spiritual, the daily bread that those who fear God shall not want and the food that endures for ever. John Wesley keeps it to necessary provisions for their being and well-being.

On the power of the works shown to the people John Gill distinguishes two showings, in fact and in prophecy: Israel saw the works in Egypt, at the sea, in the wilderness and in Canaan with their own eyes, and they were also declared beforehand, as one Jewish commentator observes, so that it might not be said they came by chance. Adam Clarke presses the same point differently, that the people could see these things did not arrive in the common course of nature, and that it required a display of divine power to give them the heritage of the heathen. Matthew Henry specifies the proofs of that power, beginning with the possession given in Canaan when the seven nations were subdued.
7:
On the works being verity and judgment John Gill divides the two words: the providences that drove out the Canaanites and settled Israel were truth, as fulfilling the promises and prophecies, and judgment, as punishment for the sins of the nations; and he reports that some refer the phrase to the two tables of stone, which were the work and writing of God, while one Jewish commentator takes it of the law implanted in the hearts of men. Adam Clarke makes the same division historically: the works were truth because wrought to fulfil what was promised to the fathers, and just because Israel and Babylon alike were punished for their own infidelities. On the standing fast Adam Clarke presses the verb, that they are propped up and buttressed for ever, since God’s power supports his works and his providence preserves the record of them. John Gill extends the permanence to law and Gospel together, and John Wesley keeps it to the constancy of the commandments.

The ninth verse gives Adam Clarke his occasion for a complaint about titles. The word we render reverend, he says, comes from the Latin and is compounded of an intensive with a verb meaning to be feared, so that the superlative form means greatly to be feared; these are now only titles of ecclesiastical respect, especially in the Protestant ministry, but there was a time when they were no empty titles — when the clergy walked not in the fear of the Lord they caused the people to fear, and when the secular power was added to the spiritual they were truly to be feared. But the word is not applied to God in that way, and the Hebrew rather means terrible: holy and tremendous is his name, a title that belongs not to man. John Wesley divides the same word three ways, terrible to enemies, venerable in his people’s eyes, and holy in all his dealings. On the redemption sent Adam Clarke counts the deliverances — the leader out of Egypt, the judges, the men who brought the people back from Babylon, and finally the Lord Jesus redeeming a whole lost world — while John Gill takes the temporal redemption as a type of the spiritual and eternal one.

The last verse turns on two words. John Gill defines the fear as not a dread of judgments but a reverential and filial affection, a fear of offending so good a Being, and notes that the phrase may be rendered the chief of wisdom rather than its beginning. C.H. Spurgeon says the same, that the word sometimes means the chief in Scripture, so that true religion is at once the first element of wisdom and its chief fruit, and calls knowing God so as to walk aright before him the greatest of all the applied sciences. On the good understanding Adam Clarke objects to the words our version supplies, since the original reads without them — good discernment to the doers — so that those who act by wisdom’s dictates discern their duty and their interest. Charles Ellicott would render it a good estimation rather than a good understanding, deciding by the parallelism and a proverb against the margin’s good success: not only is piety the beginning of wisdom, but righteousness wins good esteem, and the praise that endures is the good man’s. C.H. Spurgeon reports the same alternative without settling it, and makes obedience the proof that a man’s judgment is sound, since practical godliness is the test of wisdom.
